caption:
Some of the best hospitality improvements I’ve seen haven’t cost a restaurant a single dollar.

And this is something I talk about A LOT when I’m working with hospitality teams.

We often assume that improving the guest experience means investing in something new. New systems, more staff, better technology or another training program.

But sometimes the biggest opportunity is simply becoming more AWARE of what’s already happening around you.

Here’s what I mean.

1. Pay attention to your team’s natural strengths.

You’ve probably got someone on your team who’s brilliant at making nervous guests feel comfortable. Someone else who can read a room without saying a word. Or someone who has an incredible ability to make new staff feel welcome.

Are you recognising those strengths? Are you helping those people develop them? Are you encouraging them to share what they do naturally with the rest of the team?

2. Get specific about what great hospitality looks like.

Telling your team to “give great service” isn’t training. Talk about the little moments. How you acknowledge someone when you’re busy. How you recognise when a guest needs help without waiting to be asked. How you make someone feel comfortable when they walk through the door.

Give people something they can actually put into practice.

3. Create opportunities for your team to contribute.

Some of the best ideas come from the people doing the work every day. Ask questions, listen to their answers and give them the confidence to suggest a better way of doing something.

Because improving hospitality doesn’t always require a bigger budget. Sometimes it requires better awareness, more intentional leadership and recognising the potential that’s already sitting right in front of you.

And THAT is where some pretty incredible things can happen😉

Some of the best restaurant managers I’ve worked with were doing a hundred little things every day that nobody ever noticed.

And that’s often the point.

They’re not looking for applause. They’re looking after their people, keeping things moving, and making everyone else’s job a little easier.

If you’ve ever worked with a manager like this, you know just how lucky you were🫶

The downside of spending 20+ years in hospitality? You can’t switch that part of your brain off. 😂

I can be out for a lovely dinner, minding my own business, and somehow I’m still noticing EVERYTHING.

And I wouldn’t have it any other way.

If you’re as obsessed with restaurants and hospitality as I am, follow @alexis_guttridge You’re in good company here🥂
transcript: Here are five things I notice in restaurants that most guests probably don't. After 20 years in hospitality, I genuinely cannot help myself. One, how the staff communicate without speaking. A little nod across the room. Eye contact with the bartender. Someone stepping in before they've even asked. That's a team working together. there. Two, what happens when the manager walks onto the floor? Does everyone suddenly tense up or are they genuinely happy to see them? This tells me so much. Three, what happens when something goes wrong? Because let's face it, something always goes wrong. Do they start pointing fingers or does someone quietly step in and just fix it? Four, who's paying attention to the whole room, not just their own tables. I love watching someone notice another section, needs help, and jump in without being asked. And five, how the staff treat each other. You can put on a great performance for guests, but how people treat each other when nobody's watching. That tells me more about a restaurant than almost anything else. And once you start noticing these things, it's pretty hard to stop.

caption:
A good pre-shift can completely change the energy of a restaurant before the doors even open.

And some of the BEST ideas I’ve seen are incredibly simple.

A quick tasting. A little role-playing. Getting someone on the team to share something they’re brilliant at.

It doesn’t need to be complicated, but it DOES need to be intentional.

Restaurant people, what’s something you’ve done (or experienced) in a pre-shift that actually worked?

I’d love to steal a few good ideas. 😂
transcript: If your pre-shift meetings are just about the specials, you're missing the point. A great pre-shift should do more than tell your team what's happening tonight. It should actually prepare them for it. Here are three things I'd love to see more restaurants doing. First, get your team talking. Instead of standing there giving everyone a rundown, ask a question. What's one thing we could do better than yesterday? What's something a guest asked you recently that you didn't know the answer to? Get people contributing because if you're the only one talking for 15 minutes, I'm not sure how much anybody's actually taking in. Second, practice something. It doesn't have to be some big formal training session. Have someone describe a dish they're excited about. Practice how to respond when a guest doesn't like their wine. Let someone who's brilliant at selling desserts share how they do it. Five minutes of actually doing something can be worth a hell of a lot more than 15 minutes of listening. And third, give the team something to focus on together. Not just, let's have a great service tonight. Something specific. Maybe it's making sure every guest celebrating something feels genuinely acknowledged. Maybe it's improving how the team communicates when the restaurant gets slammed. Then here's the important part. Talk about it again tomorrow. Did it work? What did we learn? What could we do differently? Because a pre-shift shouldn't be something you do just because you've always done it. It's an opportunity to make your team a little bit better every single day. And that's a pretty valuable 15 minutes.

caption:
Someone asked me a brilliant question recently: How do you know if someone has a natural gift for hospitality BEFORE you hire them?

And I loved it because I think we spend so much time interviewing people about what they’ve DONE that we forget to find out who they ARE.

Some of the best hospitality people I’ve ever worked with weren’t necessarily the most experienced.

They were the ones who genuinely gave a shit about people.

And you can’t always spot that on a resume. 

What’s the BEST interview question you’ve ever been asked (or asked someone else)?
transcript: Here are three questions I'd ask in a restaurant interview that have absolutely nothing to do with restaurant experience. Because you can teach someone how to carry plates, open wine, or use a POS system. But I want to know who they are as a person. One, tell me about a time you made someone's day better. It doesn't have to be at work. I'm interested in whether they naturally notice opportunities to do something thoughtful for someone else. Two, what's something you're really proud of that has nothing to do with work? I love this question because people light up when they talk about something that genuinely matters to them. And three, tell me about a time you changed your mind about something. I'm looking for curiosity, self-awareness, and whether they're open to seeing things differently. And here's something just as important as the questions themselves. Don't rush to fill the awkward silence. Give people time to think. Sometimes the most interesting answers come after the pause. Because I'm not just hiring someone to do a job. I'm looking for someone who genuinely cares about people.

caption:
I’ve spent more than 20 years in hospitality, and sitting at a bar is still one of my favourite places to watch great hospitality happen.

Here are 7 things I notice almost immediately:

1. The acknowledgement. 
Even when they’re slammed, does someone make eye contact or give me a quick nod?

2. How they treat newcomers. 
Are the regulars getting all the attention, or does everyone feel welcome?

3. The menu. 
Is someone offering one, or am I left hunting for it?

4. Their awareness. 
Are they watching the entire bar, or just focused on making drinks?

5. Their recommendations. 
Do they ask what I enjoy before suggesting something?

6. The solo guest. 
Does someone sitting alone feel just as welcome as a group of six?

7. The goodbye. 
Does anyone notice when a guest leaves?

None of these things requires a fancy cocktail menu or an expensive fit-out.
Just people who genuinely understand hospitality.

🥃Bartenders, what would YOU add?

Good food gets people through the door. How you make them FEEL brings them back. 

Restaurant people, do you agree?
transcript: A restaurant can do everything right and still lose a guest. The food can be fantastic. The service can be friendly. The restaurant can look beautiful. And that guest might never come back. Because sometimes it's not about anything going wrong. It's about nothing making them feel particularly special. Think about the last restaurant you went to where everything was perfectly fine. You enjoyed your meal, you paid your bill, you left. But can you remember anything about the experience? Now think about a restaurant you absolutely love going back to. I bet there's something about the way they make you feel. Maybe someone remembers your name. Maybe they know how you like your coffee. Maybe there's a little moment of genuine connection. And here's what I want more restaurant leaders to understand. You don't always need to change your menu, renovate your space, or spend more money to give people a reason to return. Sometimes you just need to give them something worth remembering.

caption:
One of the biggest mistakes I see in restaurants? Trying to fix the problem you can see without understanding what’s causing it.

Here are a few examples of where I’d look first.

1. Staff keep leaving.
Before blaming the hiring market, I’d want to know who they’re working for, how they’re being managed, and what their first 30 days actually look like.

2. Service is inconsistent.
Before scheduling another training session, I’d look at what happens before the doors open. Are expectations clear? Is there a proper pre-shift? Does anyone follow up on what was taught yesterday?

3. Managers are burning out.
Before telling them to delegate more, I’d want to know what decisions they’re actually allowed to make. Are they empowered to lead, or does everything still have to go through the owner?

4. Guests aren’t coming back.
Before changing the menu or offering discounts, I’d look at the entire guest experience. What happens when they arrive? How do they feel when they leave? And does anyone follow up after their visit?

5. The owner can’t step away.
Before hiring another manager, I’d want to understand why the restaurant still depends on one person to make every decision.

Here’s the thing.

Sometimes the problem everyone is talking about isn’t actually the problem.

It’s just the symptom.

And if you keep fixing symptoms, you’re going to keep having the same fucking conversations six months from now 🤷‍♀️

caption:
You can learn a hell of a lot about a restaurant before the first plate ever hits the table.

Here are some of the things I notice…

1. Does anyone actually answer the phone?

And if they can’t, is there an easy way to get the information you need? I understand restaurants get busy, but trying to give someone your business shouldn’t feel like hard work.

2. Does their Instagram match the restaurant you walk into?

I’m not talking about whether the photos are beautiful. Does the personality, the atmosphere, the experience they’ve been showing you actually exist when you arrive? Or does it feel like you’ve walked into a completely different restaurant?

3. What happens in the first 30 seconds?

Does somebody acknowledge you, even if they’re busy? Do you feel like they’re genuinely happy you’ve arrived, or like you’ve just interrupted something? That first interaction can set the tone for the entire night.

4. How does the team interact with each other?

I’m ALWAYS watching this. Are they smiling, communicating, helping each other? Or does everybody look like they’re just trying to survive the shift? You can feel the difference, and it tells me a lot about what’s happening behind the scenes.

5. Does anyone seem genuinely excited about what’s happening in the restaurant?

Maybe it’s a new dish, a wine they’re loving, or just the fact that it’s a busy Friday night. I love walking into a restaurant where the team actually seems proud of the place they work.

6. What does the room feel like before you even sit down?

Is there energy? Is the music right? Is the lighting comfortable? Does the restaurant feel like someone has actually thought about how it feels to be there, not just how it looks?

And the funny thing is, I haven’t even ordered a fucking drink yet. 😂

None of these things can tell me whether the food will be good. But they tell me an awful lot about the people, the culture, and how much thought has gone into the guest experience.

caption:

Your glass is nearly empty, they catch your eye, give you a little nod, and another cocktail is on its way. No waving your arms around like you’re directing traffic.

2. When a server tells you NOT to order something.

You’re telling me you care more about my experience than squeezing another $28 out of me? Marry me.

3. When the staff have just the right amount of cheek.

A perfectly timed sarcastic comment that has the whole table losing it? I fucking LOVE those people. Give me personality over a rehearsed script any day.

4. When someone is borderline OBSESSED with something on the menu.

Not “Everything’s really good.” I want the server who practically grabs my arm because I haven’t ordered their favourite wine. THAT energy.

5. When someone acknowledges a celebration without making it weird.

A quiet congratulations. A little surprise from the kitchen. Not six staff members clapping while I contemplate crawling under the table.

6. When the outdoor tables aren’t treated like forgotten children.

I’m enjoying a cocktail, not participating in a survival challenge. I shouldn’t need to send a search party inside to order another drink. 😂

7. When someone remembers something random from my last visit.

Not my drink order. The holiday I was planning. The dog I mentioned three weeks ago. That shit gets me EVERY time.

It’s people paying attention, having a personality, and genuinely enjoying making someone else’s day better.

Those are the restaurants I fall in love with🧡

caption:
I’ve eaten in plenty of restaurants where everything was technically right and I still walked out feeling… nothing.

And I’ve eaten in places where maybe everything wasn’t perfect, but somebody made me feel so genuinely looked after that I couldn’t wait to go back.

That’s the bit I think we sometimes lose when we get really focused on standards and systems. And to be clear, I fucking love standards and systems. Restaurants need them.

But they’re supposed to give your team the confidence and consistency to actually look up from the checklist and pay attention to the person sitting in front of them.

Because your guests probably won’t remember whether you hit every single step of service.

They’ll remember how it felt to be there.

Sometimes you don’t need another person telling you how to run your restaurant.

You need someone who understands the business, isn’t caught up in the middle of it, and is willing to tell you what they actually think.

A bag, coat, umbrella, flowers, shopping. They notice you trying to solve the problem before you end up putting it on the floor or balancing it on the back of your chair.

2. A minute to actually settle in.

You’ve just walked in, taken off your coat, moved your bag, pulled out your chair. Great service reads the moment instead of immediately launching into water, specials and “Have you dined with us before?”

3. What you’ll need for the food before you need it.

The shell bowl with the prawns. Extra napkins with the ribs. A steak knife before the steak. The restaurant knows how its food is eaten. You shouldn’t have to ask.

4. Room for what’s coming next.

Don’t arrive with three dishes and then watch the guests play fucking Tetris with their own table. Great teams make the space before they need it.

5. To repeat something the restaurant already knows.

The allergy in the booking notes. The anniversary mentioned at the door. The fact that someone needs to leave by eight. Great restaurants make information travel with the guest.

6. Permission for your table to have its own pace.

Some tables want to linger. Some have theatre tickets. Some want another bottle. Some are fucking exhausted and want dessert and the bill. Great service doesn’t force every table through the exact same rhythm.

7. To be rescued from an awkward moment.

You drop your fork. Spill your drink. Mispronounce something on the menu. Walk towards the wrong door. Don’t make a guest feel stupid for needing help.

Okay, so how did I actually get better at running pre-shift?

A few things that helped me:

1. Don’t make the whole thing about what went wrong yesterday.
If every lineup is just a list of mistakes, your team will start tuning you out. Give feedback, absolutely. But give them something to feel good about too.

2. Teach ONE thing.
A dish. A wine. How you want a guest greeted. A question you want servers asking tonight. They don’t need 14 lessons before service — give them one thing they’ll actually remember.

3. Your energy goes first.
The energy you bring into lineup sets the tone. If you walk in flat, distracted or pissed off, don’t be surprised when that’s what you get back.

Think game day. The best coaches don’t walk into the room five minutes before the game and suck the life out of everyone. They get people switched on.

That doesn’t mean you need to put on some fake rah-rah performance. But if you’re having a shit day and genuinely can’t bring the energy, maybe someone else should run lineup that day.

And one I’d add now after 20+ years in hospitality: don’t wing it.

Take five minutes beforehand and decide what you actually want your team to walk away knowing, feeling or doing differently.

Running a great pre-shift is a skill.
And like I said in the reel — skills can be learned.

My first list about them became one of my most watched reels ever, so here are 17 more things I notice when regulars walk in…

1. Someone usually spots them before they’ve even made it through the door.

2. Their drink sometimes starts being made before they’ve ordered it.

3. They have a favourite seat, and somehow everyone knows which one it is.

4. They know who got promoted, who just got back from holiday and who’s having a rough week.

5. When they bring someone new, they become the unofficial tour guide. “You HAVE to order this.”

6. They notice new staff—and the good ones introduce themselves instead of expecting to be recognised.

7. Another regular gives them that little nod, even though they know nothing about each other outside the restaurant.

8. They know when the team is slammed and somehow become easier guests because of it.

10. They know when their favourite server isn’t quite themselves that night.

12. They know which nights are quiet, which are chaos and exactly when they like to come in.

13. Sometimes they know the restaurant’s history better than half the current team.

14. When the restaurant is absolutely packed, they’re genuinely happy for you.

15. They recommend the restaurant like they have shares in the place.

16. Eventually you forget when they became a regular. They’ve just… always been there.

17. Years later, you might not remember what they ordered—but you remember their name, their face and how it felt when they walked through the door.

At some point, great regulars stop feeling like customers.

They become part of the restaurant.

The longer you’ve owned it, the harder it can be to actually SEE it.

So how do you get fresh eyes on a restaurant you’ve walked into 10,000 times?

A few things I’d try:

Ask another restaurant owner.
Not for a formal audit. Buy them a coffee, walk them through your space and ask: What am I not seeing anymore?

Go somewhere completely different from yours.
Different price point. Different style. Different city if you can. Pay attention to what makes you think, shit, that’s good.

Follow businesses that aren’t your competition.
Sometimes the best ideas come from a winery, hotel, café or restaurant doing something completely different from you.

Go back to something that inspired you in the beginning.
Pick up Setting the Table again. Listen to an old hospitality podcast. Revisit the restaurant that originally made you want to do this.

Ask your team.
They’re seeing things every day that you’re probably not. Ask them one simple question: If this were your restaurant, what’s one thing you’d change?

And yes, sometimes you bring in someone like me.

But the point isn’t WHO gives you the perspective.

The point is making sure you’re still looking for it.

caption:
People assume restaurant managers eat cold meals because they’re too busy.

Sometimes that’s true. But more often, it’s because their attention is somewhere else.

They finally sit down for a bite and a server has a question. They notice a guest has left half a glass of the new Shiraz. They remember table 12 ordered the chicken and genuinely want to know what they thought of the new sauce. Then they spot a regular heading for the door and want to thank them for coming in.

When they finally get to the table, they aren’t asking, “How was everything?”

They’re asking, “What did you think of the new Shiraz?” or “How was the sauce on the chicken tonight?” because they’ve been thinking about those little details all evening.

Then they head back to the kitchen… and their dinner is cold.

Again.

I don’t think that’s because restaurant managers care less about their own meal.

I think it’s because, for the good ones, everyone else’s experience has always come first.

Most people think pre-shifts are about passing on information.

What’s on special.
Who’s booked.
What’s sold out.
Who needs to leave early.

Those things matter.

But the best pre-shifts I’ve ever seen do something else.

They remind the team what kind of experience they’re about to create.

I’ve seen restaurants with incredible food and average pre-shifts.

And I’ve seen restaurants with average food and exceptional pre-shifts.

Guess which teams usually create the better guest experience.

If you’re a restaurant owner or manager, what’s one thing you always make sure your team hears before every service?
transcript: I changed one thing and the whole restaurant felt different. I was working with a client recently when we decided to try something different. They knew the specials, they knew what was booked, they knew what had run out. But nobody was talking about the guest experience. Nobody was recognizing great work from yesterday. Nobody was reminding the team why their role mattered. So we changed one thing. Not the length of the pre-shift, the purpose of it. It wasn't about changing the meeting. It was about changing what the team walked into service thinking about.

3. They seem to know exactly when to approach the table… and, more importantly, when not to.

5. Even when they’re absolutely slammed, they rarely make you feel rushed.

6. They solve little problems before they become big ones. Most guests never even realise anything happened.

8. They never make you feel awkward for asking a question, changing your mind or needing another minute.

9. You’d never know they’re in the weeds. Somehow, they make chaos look calm.

10. They leave little moments behind that have nothing to do with the food. A joke. Remembering your name. A perfectly timed comment. Those are the things people talk about afterwards.

11. They don’t look like they’re performing hospitality. It just feels like who they are.

12. And my favourite… they’re not afraid to have a little fun. If they spot a camera, they’ll smile, wave or jump into the moment instead of pretending it isn’t there. Those tiny, genuine interactions are often what people remember most.

One of the most interesting parts of consulting is this…

Here are seven conversations I have all the time…

1. “I think it’s a staffing problem.” Most of the time, it’s actually a leadership and communication problem.

2. “We need more customers.” Sometimes. But more often, we need to give the customers you already have a better reason to come back.

3. “Our service is inconsistent.” Service usually isn’t the problem. Training and clear expectations are.

4. “Guests just aren’t spending enough.” Often they would… if the team felt more confident making recommendations.

5. “We’re flat out all the time.” Being busy and being efficient are two very different things.

6. “People keep leaving.” Before we blame pay, I always want to understand what it’s actually like to work there.

7. “I think we need to change everything.” Honestly… most restaurants don’t. They need someone to connect the dots they’ve stopped seeing.

If you’ve ever said one of these, which one was it?

5. The staff.

I watch how they communicate.
The best teams feel connected.
The worst teams feel like everyone is fighting their own battle.

6. The energy.

Restaurants should feel like controlled chaos.
Guests should never feel the chaos part.

7. The water glass.

I’d genuinely rather wait.

8. The wine glasses.

9. The cutlery.

The genius who puts a high-top table next to a standard-height table so somebody spends the entire meal staring directly at another person’s ass.
*Once you see it, you can’t unsee it.

11. Manager B.

If the restaurant is busy and the manager is parked on a laptop, my eye starts twitching.
You cannot lead hospitality from behind a screen.

12. The menu.

Before I read a single item, I’m looking at the menu itself.
Is it clean?Simple?Intentional?

Now I’m curious.

Hospitality people and guests...

What do YOU notice first when you walk into a restaurant? ↓

One of the biggest lies the restaurant industry ever sold people is that “serious” food people only want fancy food ↓

balance.
comfort.

how something actually tastes.

Atmosphere matters.

It’s about life.

You don’t lose your fire by becoming warmer.
You don’t lose your authority by being human.

The emotional side.
The dog-obsessed, heart-wide-open side too.

Grounded.
Earned in a different way.

⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
Creating Pause has given me the opportunity to use all of it. The good, the bad and the ugly to help other find balance in the workplace before the burnout happens. ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
Thank you to all of you that have helped me along this epic life journey. Each interaction. Each hug. Each smile back has made a difference in my life. And I hope to do the same for all of you. ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
With love-⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
